LD 1601: An Act to Create Parity in Poultry Processing and Farming Licenses and
Inspections

Sponsor: Representative Amanda Collamore
April 24, 2025

Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Amanda Collamore and I
have the great honor of representing House District 68, Pittsfield, Clinton, Bumham, and Troy. I
stand before you today to present LD 1601: An Act to Create Parity in Poultry Processing
and Farming Licenses and Inspections.

This bill addresses a long-standing challenge in our agricultural community: the inconsistent
application and interpretation of USDA regulations and exemptions among inspectors at the state
and local levels. These discrepancies don't just create confusion----they can impose unfair burdens on farmers and processors, lead to umecessary delays, and in some cases, risk the
viability of small, family-run operations.

There is nothing more frustrating than preparing your facilities and processes to meet the standards communicated by one inspector, only to have a different inspector the following
year----or even the following month---provide an entirely new interpretation of the very same rules. What should be a consistent and collaborative effort to ensure food safety becomes instead
an unpredictable and sometimes adversarial process.

This bill proposes the formation of a stakeholder group--one that includes farmers and
processors from every county in Maine, across a range of scales and agricultural sectors. By
including both conventional and organic farmers and producers from all l6 of Maine's counties, the bill ensures a broad representation of the real-world conditions and challenges faced by those
who grow and process our food.
The goal of this group----to create a uniform interpretation of USDA regulations and
exemptions in Maine---is both practical and deeply needed. With clear, stable, and consistent standards, farmers and processors can focus on doing what they do best: producing safe, highquality food for our communities.

Furthermore, the bill includes a five-year transition period for existing license holders to come into compliance with any new interpretations developed by the stakeholder group. This shows a
thoughtful understanding of the need for gradual implementation, and provides time for

RE: Support of LD 1601 - An Act to Create Parity in Poultry Processing and Farming Licenses and Inspections
My name is Eric Venturini and I'm the Executive Director of the Wild Blueberry Commission of Maine testifying in support of this bill.
The Wild Blueberry Commission (WBCM) works on behalf of Maine's 5121 farms who grow wild blueberries on 47,6001 acres across the State. In 2024, Maine produced approximately 85 million pounds of wild blueberries representing nearly 100% of all wild blueberries and approximately 10% of all blueberries grown in the US. Our industry contributes $361 million dollars to the state's economy annually2 and is the only state with significant commercial production of wild blueberries.
Maine's wild blueberry industry has for decades invested time and resources to maintain its impeccable food safety record, and as new technologies and best management practices are developed, has readily incorporated them to make further improvements.
That is why we are so grateful to Representative Collamore for presenting this bill which could help to provide a greater level of consistency and predictability in the interpretation and application of federal food safety laws as they apply to unique industries in Maine.
Maine's wild blueberry industry is one of, if not the, most unique cropping systems in the United States. Harvested every other year, never planted, existing as a natural contiguous mat comprised of hundreds of unique individual plants per acre--it is often hard to fit our holistic management practices into the square hole of federal regulations. This is why our industry, through our Food Safety Working Group, has invested countless hours over recent years to understand the Food Safety Modernization Act and the Produce Safety Rule, and provide education on how those laws could be interpreted to optimize practical compliance with federal rules.3
As producers adopt practices to comply with the latest federal regulations, it is essential that the interpretation and application of those regulations remain consistent. We see value in the formation of this stakeholder group and propose consideration of a friendly amendment. Applicable food safety regulations in the wild blueberry industry can vary between those processing wild blueberries and those growing wild blueberries. Therefore, we suggest that in addition to the "farmer of wild blueberries" member, the stakeholder group also include a "processor of wild blueberries" member.
Thank you for your time. On behalf of Maine's wild blueberry industry, I ask you to give this bill your support.

April 24, 2025

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Megan Patterson, Director of the Division of Animal and Plant Health within the Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources. I am speaking on behalf of the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry in opposition to LD 1601, An
Act to Create Parity in Poultry Processing and Farming Licenses and Inspections.
The Department appreciates the intent of LD 1601, which appears to be ensuring uniformity and
quality in the operation of the Maine Meat and Poultry Inspection Program (MMPI), a goal to which
we are also committed. We were here a few weeks ago speaking to LD 1198, Resolve, Directing the
Department ofAgriculture, Conservation and Forestry to Assess its Current Meat and Poultry Inspection Program, which was passed out of the Committee unanimously. As discussed at both the
public hearing and the work session for LD 1198, the Department has begun the necessary steps to
undertake this assessment, which will include holding listening sessions and administering a survey as part of our review, and the Department welcomes input from farmers, processors, and other interested
stakeholders. We are committed to meeting the report-back deadline of January 15, 2026, which
includes language allowing this Committee to submit legislation related to the report to the Second Regular Session of the l32nd Legislature.
We respectfully ask that the Department be allowed to complete the work directed by LD 1198 by the
agreed-upon deadline and not have assigmnents that appear to be duplicative added to the
Department's 360-degree review of the Program. Furthermore, we do not have the capacity to host an
ongoing stakeholder group with our existing resources.
